title:
Built a local market analysis agent that runs on a 
$0/month Oracle Cloud server — architecture notes
author: No_Progress92
selftext:
Wanted to share the architecture of something I've 

been running for a few months — a local agent that 

fetches live market data, runs deterministic analysis, 

calls an LLM, and delivers a structured brief to 

Telegram every morning before London open.



Stack:

\- Python on Oracle Cloud Free Tier (Ampere A1, Ubuntu 22.04)

\- Twelve Data API for quotes + 4H historical candles

\- analysis\_engine.py for EMA, RSI, ATR, swing structure, BOS/CHoCH

\- Claude API (haiku model — \~$0.01 per run)

\- telegram\_bot.py with MarkdownV2 formatting + retry logic

\- [scheduler.py](http://scheduler.py) with weekday-only logic and retry on failure

\- systemd service for auto-restart on reboot

\- report\_store.py archives every run as JSONL with quality score



Total cost: $0/month server, \~$3/year in API credits 

at one analysis per day.



A few design decisions worth noting:



1. Python calculates everything deterministically first. 

The LLM only sees computed facts, not raw prices. This 

killed the hallucination problem completely.



2. Mock mode (--mock --dry-run) lets you run the full 

pipeline locally with fixture data before you have any 

live credentials. Useful for testing prompt changes.



3. Every run gets archived with the prompt version, 

model output, and a quality score. Easy to spot when 

a prompt change degraded output.



4. The systemd service restarts automatically on crash 

or reboot. Has missed zero scheduled runs in production.



Happy to answer questions about any part of the 

architecture.

comments.author: New_Mode_7598
comments.body: Are you able to get profitable triggers… as LLM based trading signals are ambiguous in my experience. It gives probabilities of going each way

replies.author: No_Progress92
replies.body:
Yeah I get what you mean. Pure LLM signals are usually too soft and end up giving you probabilities in both directions.
What worked better for me was not letting the model decide the trade by itself. It only sees structured data and has to follow a strict output format. The actual trigger still has to pass clear rules.
Without that, you’re right it stays ambiguous.

replies.author: peeeanuts
replies.body: I don’t use the LLM for triggers either. With OpenCandle, I keep it on the research side, then make the actual trading decision myself.

comments.author: New_Mode_7598
comments.body: Have you tried neural network set up to identify bottoms on daily basis..

replies.author: No_Progress92
replies.body:
Not in a pure form yet.

I’ve mostly stayed away from letting a neural net directly call bottoms because they can overfit hard on daily data and still struggle when the regime changes.

Right now the system uses structured signals + clear rules for the actual trigger. A neural net for bottom detection is something I’ve thought about adding as an extra filter, but I haven’t tested a full daily setup yet.

Have you had better luck with that approach?
